name.text: Calculating expected frequencies from medical diagnostic tests

questiontext.text:
A clinic in Kisumu uses a rapid diagnostic test for malaria. Historical data shows that {@num_D@}% of patients presenting with a fever at this clinic actually have malaria.

The test is highly effective, but not perfect:

  • It correctly identifies malaria in {@num_TP@}% of cases where the patient actually has malaria (a True Positive).
  • It correctly gives a negative result in {@num_TN@}% of cases where the patient does not have malaria (a True Negative).

a) Find the probability that a randomly selected patient presenting with a fever tests positive.

(Enter your answer as an exact decimal).

\(P(\text{Positive}) =\) [[input:ans1]]

[[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

b) Out of a batch of {@pop_size@} patients presenting with a fever, estimate how many will test positive but do not actually have malaria (False Positives).

(Enter your answer as a whole number).

\(\text{Expected False Positives} =\) [[input:ans2]]

[[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution:

First, convert all percentages to exact decimal probabilities:

  • \(P(\text{Malaria}) = {@str_P_M@}\)
  • \(P(\text{No Malaria}) = 1 - {@str_P_M@} = {@str_P_NM@}\)
  • \(P(\text{Positive} \mid \text{Malaria}) = {@str_P_Pos_given_M@}\)
  • \(P(\text{Negative} \mid \text{No Malaria}) = {@str_P_Neg_given_NM@}\)

We must also find the False Positive rate (testing positive when you do not have malaria):
\(P(\text{Positive} \mid \text{No Malaria}) = 1 - P(\text{Negative} \mid \text{No Malaria}) = 1 - {@str_P_Neg_given_NM@} = {@str_P_Pos_given_NM@}\)

Part a: Probability of a Positive Result
A patient can test positive via two different paths: (Malaria and Positive) OR (No Malaria and Positive).

\( \displaystyle P(\text{Malaria and Positive}) = {@str_P_M@} \times {@str_P_Pos_given_M@} = {@str_path1@} \)

\( \displaystyle P(\text{No Malaria and Positive}) = {@str_P_NM@} \times {@str_P_Pos_given_NM@} = {@str_path2@} \)

Add these probabilities together:

\( \displaystyle P(\text{Positive}) = {@str_path1@} + {@str_path2@} \)

\( \displaystyle \boxed{ P(\text{Positive}) = {@str_ta1@} } \)

Part b: Expected False Positives
A false positive occurs on the (No Malaria and Positive) path, which has a probability of \({@str_path2@}\).
To find the expected number out of \({@pop_size@}\) patients, multiply the probability by the total population:

\( \displaystyle \text{Expected False Positives} = {@str_path2@} \times {@pop_size@} \)

\( \displaystyle \boxed{ \text{Expected} = {@ta2@} \text{ patients} } \)

The tree diagram:

[[jsxgraph width="460px" height="182px"]] (function() { var L1 = [['Malaria', '{#str_P_M#}'],['No malaria', '{#str_P_NM#}']], L2 = [[['Positive', '{#str_P_Pos_given_M#}'],['Negative', '{#float(1-P_Pos_given_M)#}']],[['Positive', '{#str_P_Pos_given_NM#}'],['Negative', '{#str_P_Neg_given_NM#}']]], LV = ['{#str_path1#}','{#float(P_M*(1-P_Pos_given_M))#}','{#str_path2#}','{#float(P_NM*P_Neg_given_NM)#}']; var n = 4, wide = LV.length ? 15 : 12; var b = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, {boundingbox:[-0.4, n + 0.4, wide, 0.3], axis:false, grid:false, showNavigation:false, showCopyright:false, pan:{enabled:false}, zoom:{enabled:false}}); function lab(p, q, t, txt) { // t: how far along the branch the label sits // probability label 55% along the branch, above an upward branch and below a downward one var x = p[0] + t*(q[0]-p[0]), y = p[1] + t*(q[1]-p[1]); var off = (q[1] >= p[1]) ? 0.32 : -0.32; b.create('text', [x, y + off, txt], {anchorX:'middle', anchorY:'middle', fontSize:13, fixed:true, strokeColor:'#1565c0'}); } var y = n, k = 0, root = [0, (n + 1)/2]; b.create('point', root, {name:'', size:3, fixed:true, color:'#333', showInfobox:false}); for (var i = 0; i < L1.length; i++) { var m = L2[i].length, ymid = y - (m - 1)/2, p1 = [3.0, ymid]; b.create('segment', [root, p1], {strokeColor:'#555', fixed:true}); lab(root, p1, 0.55, L1[i][1]); b.create('text', [3.15, ymid, L1[i][0]], {anchorY:'middle', fontSize:15, fixed:true}); for (var j = 0; j < m; j++) { var s2 = [6.3, ymid], p2 = [9.2, y]; b.create('segment', [s2, p2], {strokeColor:'#555', fixed:true}); lab(s2, p2, 0.72, L2[i][j][1]); b.create('text', [9.35, y, L2[i][j][0]], {anchorY:'middle', fontSize:15, fixed:true}); if (LV.length) b.create('text', [12.0, y, LV[k]], {anchorY:'middle', fontSize:13, fixed:true, strokeColor:'#2e7d32'}); y -= 1; k++; } } })(); [[/jsxgraph]]

questionnote.text: P(M)={@str_P_M@}, P(+|M)={@str_P_Pos_given_M@}, P(-|NM)={@str_P_Neg_given_NM@}. P(+)={@str_ta1@}. Expected FP out of {@pop_size@} = {@ta2@}

questiondescription.text:
This question is based on the example A Malaria Diagnostic Test in the section Probability in Real Life of the CBC Grade 11 Mathematics textbook (INNODEMS).

Probability in Real Life: Expected Frequencies

truefeedback.text: Correct. You successfully added the probability of a True Positive to the probability of a False Positive.

node.description: Check if they only calculated True Positives

truefeedback.text: You only calculated the probability of a True Positive (having malaria and testing positive). A patient can also test positive if they do not have malaria (a False Positive). You must calculate both paths and add them together.

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect. Review the probabilities of both paths that lead to a positive result.

truefeedback.text: Excellent. You correctly multiplied the terminal path probability by the total patient population.

node.description: Check if they ignored the population rate

truefeedback.text: You multiplied the total population directly by the conditional false positive rate. You must remember that only a fraction of the population does not have malaria in the first place. You must multiply the total population by the combined path probability of (No Malaria AND Positive).

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect. Multiply the total number of patients by the probability of the (No Malaria AND Positive) path.
